The coalition said the exercise was transparent, merit-based and technology-driven, warning that continued interference could undermine institutional stability, national security and public confidence in government recruitment.
Its position was contained in a statement jointly signed by the National Coordinator of the Coalition of Civil Society Organisations for Good Governance, Transparency and National Development, Comrade Dr Aminu Sani, and its National Secretary, Comrade Lukman Lawal, ahead of a world press conference.
The coalition, which comprises more than 33 civil society organisations, youth groups, student bodies and professional associations across the six geopolitical zones, said it monitored the recruitment exercise through independent observation, engagements with applicants and a review of published guidelines.
According to the group, more than 573,680 Nigerians from the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory applied for the exercise.
It said applicants passed through several stages of screening, including online application and verification, computer-based tests, physical screening, medical examinations, drug tests and credential verification.
At the end of the exercise, 3,852 candidates were selected across three cadres: 1,275 superintendent officers, 367 inspectorate officers and 2,210 customs assistants.
The coalition described the exercise as one of the most transparent and technology-driven recruitment processes conducted by a paramilitary agency in recent years.
It said: “The advertisement, criteria and timelines were made public. No application was conducted in secrecy.
“Selection was primarily based on performance in the CBT and subsequent screening. The process significantly reduced the influence of godfatherism, manual manipulation and backdoor recruitment.”
The group added that the use of technology and electronic verification helped limit human interference, while successful candidates emerged from different parts of the country.
It also commended the Customs Service for establishing a complaint and review mechanism for applicants who felt aggrieved by the process.
